node.label: Niall Ferguson
node.date_label: The Pity of War (1998) · Empire: How Britain Made the Modern World (2003) · The Shock of the Global: four-editor collection (2010)
node.description: A historian of war, finance and empire whose work makes counterfactual comparison explicit. In his 2007 conversation with Huw Spanner he argues that historians should state plausible alternatives rather than narrate outcomes as inevitable. He uses that approach to defend a disputed interpretation of Britain’s intervention in 1914 and to appraise imperial outcomes. These judgments remain Ferguson’s claims, including their chosen comparisons and values; the entry does not adopt them as settled verdicts on war or empire. His co-editorship of The Shock of the Global is separately credited.

incident_edges.relationship: Uses an explicit counterfactual about British nonintervention in 1914 to contest an inevitable-war narrative.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Own 2007 interview answers on alternative futures and The Pity of War. His judgment that a German victory would have been tolerable remains disputed testimony, not this graph’s endorsed conclusion or a current strategic recommendation.

incident_edges.relationship: Argues that causal explanations should state plausible alternative outcomes and preserve contemporaries’ uncertainty.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Own answers to the causation, scientific-method and counterfactual questions. A methodological proposal about explanation, not proof that counterfactuals can be experimentally tested or that every imagined alternative is plausible.

incident_edges.relationship: Uses Ferguson’s Virtual History essay as a reference for the situated character of historical judgments.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Own first-chapter note17 and attached observer/judgment paragraph, with Evans, Appleby/Hunt/Jacob, Bloch and Carr co-credited. This is a specific cited methodological resource, not a claim Gaddis endorses every counterfactual or Ferguson’s imperial arguments. Original Ferguson essay and remainder of the edited collection unread; edition year not inferred from shortened Gaddis note.

named_group_routes.relationship: Cites Telling the Truth about History in acknowledging the situated character of historical judgment.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Own first-chapter passage beginning We have, in recent years, embraced postmodernist insights, and note17, co-credit Joyce Appleby and Margaret Jacob as authors of the1994book and also cite Evans/Ferguson/Bloch/Carr. Note24 additionally references the jointly authored book for observer/reconstruction problems. No soleHuntauthorship, no general pupil genealogy, no claim that all these scholars share one theory; original jointbook unread.
